TextView.android:text: Intermediate Lesson 14: Notable Points & Lines in Geometry

If you take ANY point P inside a triangle and drop perpendiculars to the three sides, the feet of these perpendiculars form a new triangle called the 'Pedal Triangle'. \nHowever, something magical happens if point P lies ON THE CIRCUMCIRCLE of the original triangle. The three feet of the perpendiculars no longer form a triangle; instead, they lie on a single straight line! This is called the Simson Line.\nMoreover, the Simson line of point P always bisects the line segment connecting P to the Orthocenter (H) of the triangle.

Miquel's Theorem is a beautiful statement about circles associated with a triangle. \nIf you choose three arbitrary points D, E, and F on the sides BC, CA, and AB of a triangle ABC, then the three circumcircles of triangles AFE, BDF, and CED will ALWAYS intersect at a single common point. This point is called the Miquel Point.\nIf the points D, E, F are collinear, the Miquel point lies on the circumcircle of ABC.

Take ANY quadrilateral (convex, concave, or even self-intersecting) and connect the midpoints of its four sides in order. 
Varignon's Theorem states that the resulting shape is ALWAYS a Parallelogram!
The area of this Varignon parallelogram is exactly HALF the area of the original quadrilateral. 
If the original quadrilateral has equal diagonals, the Varignon shape is a Rhombus. If the diagonals are perpendicular, it is a Rectangle.

A Median connects a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. If you reflect the Median across the Angle Bisector of that same vertex, you get a new, extremely important line called the Symmedian.\nJust like medians intersect at the Centroid, the three Symmedians of a triangle intersect at a single point called the Lemoine Point (or Symmedian Point).\nThe Lemoine point is the unique point inside the triangle that minimizes the sum of the squares of its distances to the three sides.
The midpoints of the sides of a convex quadrilateral of area 200 form a new quadrilateral. What is the area of this new inner quadrilateral?

Solution: By Varignon's Theorem, the quadrilateral formed by connecting the midpoints of the sides of ANY quadrilateral is a parallelogram. \nA secondary property of this theorem proves that the area of the Varignon parallelogram is exactly half the area of the original quadrilateral. \nArea = 200 / 2 = 100.
Point P lies on the circumcircle of an equilateral triangle ABC. Perpendiculars are dropped from P to sides AB, BC, and CA, meeting them at points D, E, and F. What shape do points D, E, and F form?

Solution: This is the exact definition of the Simson Line. Because point P lies precisely on the circumcircle of the triangle, the feet of the perpendiculars do not form a shape (triangle). Instead, they are perfectly collinear. \nThey form a straight line.
